assertion: An event exists, described as "World Cup 2026 hydration breaks".
judge_quote: players at the World Cup 2026 in the US, Canada and Mexico are being given additional, but controversial hydration breaks 22 minutes into each half.
evidence_cited: It's one reason why players at the World Cup 2026 in the US, Canada and Mexico are being given additional, but controversial hydration breaks 22 minutes into each half.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Record temperatures this summer".
judge_quote: record temperatures on their way this summer thanks to a powerful El Niño weather pattern
evidence_cited: And with record temperatures on their way this summer thanks to a powerful El Niño weather pattern, it's likely to be a tough time to exercise.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Research warns of premature deaths".
judge_quote: García-Witulski and colleagues have recently warned in new research that rising temperatures due to climate change could lead to people moving less in the heat and consequentially result in an estimated 470,000 to 700,000 premature deaths per year by 2050.
evidence_cited: García-Witulski and colleagues have recently warned in new research that rising temperatures due to climate change could lead to people moving less in the heat and consequentially result in an estimated 470,000 to 700,000 premature deaths per year by 2050.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Body cools during exercise".
justification: Article describes cooling mechanisms but not an event named "Body cools during exercise"
evidence_cited: As you work out, your muscles contract and generate heat. Your body then tries to cool itself by sweating and diverting blood towards the skin.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Blood robbed from muscles".
justification: Article presents it as a claim, not an event
evidence_cited: But that creates a trade-off as the same blood is also needed to supply oxygen to your muscles, says Ollie Jay from the University of Sydney. "Your skin is basically robbing blood from your muscles, so you can't deliver as much oxygen to them."

assertion: An event exists, described as "Fatigue and heart strain".
justification: Article mentions fatigue and heart strain as effects, not as an event
evidence_cited: In hot conditions, can very quickly lead to fatigue as your body struggles to get enough oxygen to your muscles, but it can also put extra strain on your heart as it tries to keep up with the demand.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Exercise when cooler".
justification: Article gives advice to exercise when cooler, not an event
evidence_cited: The single most impactful change most people can make is to exercise when it is cooler, such as in the morning or evening, if this is possible.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Choose shaded areas".
justification: Article advises choosing shade, not an event
evidence_cited: You could also pick times when the area where you like to exercise is in the shade as opposed to the full glare of the Sun. "That difference can be as much as 12-15C (22-27F) higher than the shaded air temperature," says Ollie Jay, director of the Heat and Health Research Centre at the University of Sydney.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Consider humidity and wind".
justification: Article discusses humidity and wind, not an event
evidence_cited: Humidity matters too. Your body's primary way of losing heat is through sweat evaporating from the skin, which helps to lower your body temperature. But in humid conditions, that process is affected as the evaporation that cools your body reduces. Wind speed also plays a role, which is why running in enclosed spaces with little airflow makes heat stress a bigger risk.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Shorten exercise and add breaks".
justification: Article suggests shortening exercise and adding breaks, not an event
evidence_cited: On days when you can't avoid the heat, you might consider exercising for shorter periods of time as well as adding in more breaks.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Cool down in breaks".
justification: Article advises cooling down during breaks, not an event
evidence_cited: Rebecca Stearns, a kinesiologist at the Korey Stringer Institute at the University of Connecticut says that while taking breaks from exercise, find a cooler environment where possible. "If you can get inside an air-conditioned environment, or even just shade with cold water and a fan, take time to actually start to cool down," she says.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Heat tool developed".
judge_quote: Jay and colleagues at the University of Sydney have developed a free heat tool covering over 40 sports that draws on your local weather data.
evidence_cited: (For those who want to check their potential heat stress risk, Jay and colleagues at the University of Sydney have developed a free heat tool covering over 40 sports that draws on your local weather data.)

assertion: An event exists, described as "Use immersion cooling".
justification: Article mentions immersion cooling as a method, not an event
evidence_cited: Immersion cooling can be a better way to cool down. This is where you submerge parts of the body (such as the hands and forearms) in cold water. Alternatively, you can pour water over yourself.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Apply water to skin".
justification: Article mentions applying water to skin as a method, not an event
evidence_cited: "If you take water and apply it to the skin surface, and then that water evaporates, that's actually doing the job of sweating without having to sweat," says Jay. That then means your body can direct more blood to your muscles to deliver oxygen.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Use cold wet towel".
justification: Article mentions using a cold wet towel as a method, not an event
evidence_cited: Similarly, a cold wet towel frequently rotated over your arms, legs and torso also helps cool you down, says Stearns.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Pre-cool before exercise".
justification: Article advises pre‑cooling, not an event
evidence_cited: Pre-cooling before you head out is also helpful. Research shows that reducing body temperature before exercise gives you a greater heat buffer before conditions become dangerous. "Slightly lowering your body temperature before you go into the heat will give you a greater amount of time before it becomes dangerous," Stearns says.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Consume ice slurry".
justification: Article mentions consuming ice slurry as a method, not an event
evidence_cited: This can also be done by consuming ice slurry (icy water), which has been found to cool the body and improve exercise performance.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Heat acclimatisation".
justification: Article describes heat acclimatisation as a process, not an event
evidence_cited: Gradually building up the amount of exercise you do in hot weather will allow your body get used to it, a process called heat acclimatisation.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Adaptations after 7-14 days".
justification: Article describes adaptations after 7‑14 days, not an event
evidence_cited: Generally, says Stearns, after seven to 14 days of regularly exercising in the heat your core temperature at rest drops, your sweat rate rises and your blood plasma volume increases. "You have this huge demand for blood flow. And blood is ultimately what's going to be able to supply and support all of these physiological functions in the heat," she says.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Adaptations are transient".
justification: Article states adaptations are transient, not an event
evidence_cited: But this response is "transient", says Jay. "If you don't use it, you'll lose it… If you don't expose yourself to the heat, then those adaptations that you've primed will disappear."

assertion: An event exists, described as "Heat exhaustion becoming common".
justification: Article notes heat exhaustion is becoming more common, not an event
evidence_cited: While fatalities from exercising in the heat are relatively rare, heat exhaustion is becoming more common.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Elite athletes at higher risk".
justification: Article says elite athletes are at higher risk, not an event
evidence_cited: Elite athletes can be at a higher risk of heatstroke than recreational exercisers because they are already used to pushing themselves "past their biological limits", says Stearns. This could be dangerous as the intensity of the exercise is the primary driver of rising internal body temperature.

assertion: An event exists, described as "Listen to your body".
justification: Article advises listening to your body, not an event
evidence_cited: She therefore advises that "listening to your body and deliberately backing off the pace is your primary line of defence".

assertion: An event exists, described as "Stop if symptoms appear".
justification: Article advises stopping if symptoms appear, not an event
evidence_cited: Heat related illness is still a risk so signs to look out for include dizziness, nausea, fatigue and palpitations. If any of these appear, stop immediately and cool down.

assertion: A claim exists, described as "Heat makes exercise harder".
judge_quote: "Walking, cycling, exercising outdoors and even daily routines like commuting on foot become more physically demanding and less comfortable when temperatures are high," says Christian García-Witulski
evidence_cited: "Walking, cycling, exercising outdoors and even daily routines like commuting on foot become more physically demanding and less comfortable when temperatures are high," says Christian García-Witulski, an environmental lifestyle epidemiologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Argentina.

assertion: A claim exists, described as "Reduced activity harms health".
judge_quote: But if we reduce our physical activity each time it feels too hot to exercise outside, it can contribute to long-term health risks.
evidence_cited: But if we reduce our physical activity each time it feels too hot to exercise outside, it can contribute to long-term health risks.

assertion: A claim exists, described as "Shorter walks safer".
judge_quote: "Sometimes a shorter walk in the morning, or some light indoor movement, is safer and more realistic than trying to stick rigidly to the same routine," says García-Witulski.
evidence_cited: "Sometimes a shorter walk in the morning, or some light indoor movement, is safer and more realistic than trying to stick rigidly to the same routine," says García-Witulski. "Hotter conditions create more thermal strain. People tire more easily, sweat more, may feel dizzy or uncomfortable, often sleep worse and daily movement simply becomes less appealing and, in some cases, less safe."

assertion: A claim exists, described as "Ice packs low cooling rate".
judge_quote: While ice packs feel cold to the skin they actually have a surprisingly low cooling rate because they tend to only cover a small part of the skin.
evidence_cited: But Stearns says that while ice packs feel cold to the skin they actually have a surprisingly low cooling rate because they tend to only cover a small part of the skin.

assertion: A claim exists, described as "Exercise not separate from climate".
judge_quote: "I think the bigger message is that we should stop thinking of physical activity as something completely separate from climate," says García-Witulski.
evidence_cited: "I think the bigger message is that we should stop thinking of physical activity as something completely separate from climate," says García-Witulski. "As heatwaves become more common, people will increasingly need to adapt not just whether they move, but when, where, and how they do it," he adds.
